idiom_name: context struct plus static step functions (explicit this-pointer)
implementation_notes: C has neither member functions nor closures, so the classic structure is written by hand: put the receiver, the arguments and the former locals into a struct (the context), then turn each extracted step into a static function whose first parameter is a pointer to that context; the original function creates the context on the stack and calls the steps. Keep the struct and the helpers private to the translation unit (static) so the algorithm stays an implementation detail of the module. The context only replaces a method object when the steps really share that state - a helper that needs two values should keep taking them as parameters.
pitfalls: The context has no lifetime management of its own: returning a pointer to a stack context dangles, and a heap-allocated one leaks unless the same function frees it after the last step.
Nothing in the language stops the steps from being called out of order or on a half-initialised context; document the invariants and assert them.
Turning the private context into a module-wide struct (or passing it through a void pointer) destroys the encapsulation the extraction was meant to preserve.
